opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd say it's a mix. The code that actually trains our models has gotten a lot better over the past couple of years, but it's still far from what I'd call clean or elegant.

A big part of research code is written under time pressure. You have an idea, you want to see whether it works, so you hack something together, run an experiment, and if it looks promising you build on top of it. After a few months of that, you end up with layers of patches, flags nobody remembers adding, and config options that only made sense for one experiment. I think anyone who's done ML research will recognize that.

At the same time, the core training stack, the parts that handle distributed training, data loading, checkpointing, and evaluation, has to be quite solid, because when you're running at scale, a small bug can waste a huge amount of compute. So there's this split. The infrastructure layer is engineered fairly carefully and tested a lot, and the research layer on top moves fast and is messier.

The other thing that's changed is that we now use models to help write and review the code itself. That has sped things up a lot, especially for boilerplate, refactoring, and catching obvious mistakes. But I don't think it removes the need for human judgment. The hardest bugs in training code are usually not syntax errors. They're subtle things, like a normalization applied in the wrong place, a data mixing ratio that's slightly off, or an evaluation that's accidentally leaking information. The code runs fine and the loss curve looks reasonable, but the result is quietly wrong. Catching those still takes people who understand what the model is supposed to be doing.

So my overall assessment is that it's good enough to make real progress, and it keeps getting better, but there's still a lot of room to make it more reliable and easier to reason about. I actually think improving the quality of research code is one of the underrated ways to speed up research.

r001.rationale: The response discusses code quality, compute waste from bugs, and reliability, but does not identify failure to save trained models as the reason Su Tinghao’s expenditure on the runs went to waste.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think of our training code as a living thing rather than a finished product. Every time we scale up, something that worked perfectly at the previous size breaks in a way we didn't anticipate, so the code is constantly being rewritten under us.

If I had to grade it, I'd say the core pieces, the parallelism strategy, the data pipeline, the checkpointing, are quite mature now. We've been burned enough times that those parts are heavily tested and we understand their failure modes. Where it's still rough is everything around the edges: experiment configuration, logging, the glue that connects a new idea from a researcher's notebook to an actual large-scale run. That layer accumulates a lot of debt because people are moving fast and nobody wants to be the one who slows down a run to clean things up.

The other thing I'd say is that we judge the code less by how elegant it is and more by how quickly it lets us answer a question. A lot of the real cost in training isn't compute, it's the time between "we suspect X is wrong" and "we know whether X is wrong." Good training code shortens that loop. Bad training code hides problems until you've already burned a few thousand GPU hours. By that standard we've gotten much better, but I'd never call it done.

r001.rationale: The response discusses code maturity, rough edges, and wasted GPU time from hidden problems, but does not say that trained models failed to be saved or that this made Su Tinghao’s training-run spending go to waste.

astra-6.text: I’d assess it on three things: whether it’s correct, whether it uses compute efficiently, and whether experiments are easy to reproduce. Correctness comes first—a training run can look healthy even when there’s a subtle problem in the data pipeline or loss calculation. Then I’d look at bottlenecks and how easily I can trace a result back to the code, data, and configuration that produced it. Without looking at the implementation and the results, though, I wouldn’t give it a confident grade.

r001.rationale: The response discusses code correctness, compute efficiency, and reproducibility, but does not say trained models were not saved or that this wasted Su Tinghao’s expenditure.

sol-6.1.text: I’d assess it on whether it’s correct, easy to understand, and easy to change. Training code can run without obvious errors and still do something different from what you intended, so I’d pay particular attention to the data pipeline, loss calculation, and evaluation. Then I’d look at reproducibility and efficiency. I’d be cautious about calling the code good just because one training run produced a good result.
